title: Longitudinal trends in master track and field performance throughout the aging process: 83,209 results from Sweden in 16 athletics disciplines
authors: Ganse B, Kleerekoper A, Knobe M, Hildebrand F, Degens H
population: 34,132 masters track and field athletes (aged 35-97) with 83,209 results; longitudinal subset with 10+ results
findings: Performance in cross-sectional data was lower than in longitudinal data in all events except 1000 m men, because average age was lower in the cross-sectional data (men 46 vs 58, women 44 vs 56).
The annual percentage rate of decline did not differ significantly between cross-sectional and longitudinal data, or between sexes in most disciplines.
Performance declines after age 70 were 1.7 times (men) and 1.4 times (women) as steep as before.
The authors conclude cross-sectional data give a good impression of the annual percentage decline in performance, which was similar in men and women.
limitations: Track and field results (not mainly distance road running); athletes with many results are survivors, selecting for higher performers; no training data.
implications: Cross-sectional age curves can be used as a reasonable approximation of individual annual percentage decline for projecting age-based target changes.
Apply a steeper decline after age 70 (about 1.4-1.7 times the pre-70 slope) in long-range projections and goal-time realism checks.
Use no sex-specific decline slope as the default; sex differences in annual percentage decline were not significant in most disciplines.

verification.notes: Crossref and Europe PMC abstract match; numbers confirmed verbatim.
